extracted.intended_audience: attorneys practicing before the USPTO in trademark matters (including sponsoring attorneys and their support staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules governing attorney conduct, signature/account procedures, supervision, and certification when preparing, signing, and filing trademark documents via TEAS before the USPTO, plus related sanctions and reinstatement conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any foreign-domiciled trademark applicant or registrant must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney licensed to practice law in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented to increase compliance with U.S. trademark law, improve accuracy of submissions, and safeguard integrity of the trademark register. See Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney for Foreign Trademark Applicants and Registrants, 84 Fed. Reg. 31498 (July 2, 2019).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of USPTO.gov account for TEAS filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Save for specified exceptions, one must have and use a USPTO.gov account to submit trademark documents via TEAS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account holders agree to the Trademark Verified USPTO.gov Account Agreement. Attorneys may have their own accounts and may sponsor accounts for a reasonable number of support staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account holder responsibility not to share credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: An account holder agrees not to permit others to use the trademark Verified USPTO.gov account login credentials and to take reasonable steps to prevent others from learning such account login information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account holders must promptly notify the USPTO if credentials have been used by others and may not use accounts in connection with the unauthorized practice of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on who an attorney may sponsor
rubrics_metrics.description: As an attorney, I may only sponsor attorney support staff under my supervision employed or retained by my individual law practice, law firm, or as employees of the same company; I will not attempt to sponsor any other individuals or organizations, including any foreign or domestic company, group, client, agent, attorney or other practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsorship beyond permitted categories (e.g., sponsoring a foreign company, referring entity, or client) is prohibited by the USPTO Trademark Verified USPTO.gov Account Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsoring attorney verification duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A sponsoring attorney is responsible for verifying the identity of any person he or she sponsors; the identity information is subject to the account agreement terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification and recordkeeping obligations are part of the sponsoring attorney's duties under the account agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsoring attorney responsibility for conduct of sponsored users
rubrics_metrics.description: A sponsoring attorney accepts personal, professional, and ethical responsibility for the conduct of each attorney support staff when using a sponsored USPTO.gov account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney must take reasonable steps to ensure sponsored staff are familiar with the Agreement and relevant laws/regulations, that access/use is consistent with assigned tasks, promptly remove sponsorship when appropriate, immediately remove and report suspected misuse (including knowingly submitting false statements or signatures), and ensure each sponsored staff has a separate account (no sharing).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a),(c),(e); 11.18(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures on trademark documents must be signed by a proper person; trademark documents must be personally signed by the signatory named on the document; an electronic signatory must personally enter the adopted signature characters between two forward slash (/) symbols on the electronic submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP § 611.01(c): the named signatory must personally sign the printed form or personally enter his or her electronic signature; another person (e.g., paralegal) may not sign or enter the name of a qualified U.S. attorney; typing another person's electronic signature is not a valid signature. Noncompliant signatures may subject the trademark to cancellation or invalidate a registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three permitted signature methods for TEAS filings
rubrics_metrics.description: TEAS allows three signature methods: DIRECT, H-SIGN, and E-SIGN ON, each with specific requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DIRECT: default; named signatory personally enters signature on form (and if saved for later, the signature is not saved and must be reentered personally). H-SIGN: submit an electronic file (e.g., JPG/PDF) of original wet signature attached to the application. E-SIGN ON: USPTO sends a hyperlink via email to the designated signatory who opens and electronically signs the form via the link.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 certifications (truthfulness and reasonable inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: By presenting a document to the USPTO, the party represents that statements on the party's own knowledge are true and statements made on information and belief are believed to be true, and that the signatory makes certifications formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific assertions in use-based applications (ownership, use in commerce, specimen accuracy, application filing date facts) are covered. Certification elements include: (i) paper not presented for improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions warranted or nonfrivolous; (iii) factual contentions have evidentiary support or likely will after investigation; (iv) denials of factual contentions are warranted. Certification violations may jeopardize probative value; knowingly false statements can be criminally punished under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry requirement into client signatures (under § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must, after a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances, ensure factual contentions (including how client signatures were obtained) have evidentiary support or are likely to after investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to make reasonable inquiry into how clients' signatures were obtained (e.g., reliance on third-party assertions without direct contact) can violate § 11.18 and jeopardize filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation—this includes understanding USPTO trademark signature rules, the U.S. Counsel Rule, and requirements for USPTO.gov accounts and sponsored accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes possessing an adequate understanding so as not to permit non-practitioner assistants to enter named signatories' signatures, to comply with the user agreement, to adequately supervise assistants, and to make reasonable inquiries into signatures and filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must act with reasonable diligence—this includes adequately understanding signature rules and the U.S. Counsel Rule, supervising sponsored assistants, making reasonable inquiries, and adequately reviewing trademark documents prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failing diligence: engaging in reviews that were 'not robust enough', allowing assistants to enter client or attorney signatures, or presenting documents not signed in compliance with signature rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision responsibilities for non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.503(b),(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who sponsors non-practitioner assistants must adequately supervise them, ensure they are familiar with relevant laws/policies, and must not direct, allow, or facilitate them to enter client signatures on filed documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to supervise that results in non-practitioner assistants entering named signatories' signatures violates these responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on assisting unauthorized practice of law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not assist in the unauthorized practice of law, including failing to supervise sponsored non-practitioner assistants such that they practice without authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsoring or enabling non-practitioners to perform attorney functions (e.g., entering client attestations improperly) can constitute assisting unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation and conduct prejudicial to the trademark system (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.804(c) and 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting trademark documents not signed by the named signatory is conduct involving misrepresentation and conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the trademark system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of prejudicial conduct include: inadequate understanding of signature/U.S. Counsel rules, improper sponsorship of accounts, inadequate supervision, failing reasonable inquiries into client signatures, presenting noncompliant signatures, inadequate document review, and facilitating non-practitioner entries of client signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for noncompliant signatures and false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: If a signature fails to comply with 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a) or (e) because it was entered by someone other than the named signatory or not signed by a proper person, the trademark may be subject to cancellation and a resulting registration may be invalid; knowingly and willfully false or fraudulent statements are subject to criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities include the Federal Register (84 Fed. Reg. at 31498) and TTAB/Commissioner decisions (In re Dermahose Inc., In re Cowan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner monitoring duty (search and report)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are reasonably expected to search the USPTO's online trademark search system for applications identifying them as attorney of record and promptly inform the USPTO in writing of filings made without their knowledge or consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an agreed probationary condition, the Respondent must: (p) bi-weekly search tmsearch and inform Office of Trademark Examination Policy of filings made without knowledge/consent; (q) submit quarterly written reports to OED confirming searches and any notifications. Generally, practitioners should search by first and last name at https://tmsearch.uspto.gov/search/search-information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on USPTO.gov account privileges during suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: While suspended and until reinstated, Respondent shall not apply for, obtain, verify, sponsor, or use USPTO verified Electronic System accounts, and the USPTO is authorized to disable or suspend any USPTO.gov accounts registered to Respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent is prohibited from accessing, sponsoring, verifying credentials for, or using any USPTO.gov accounts for preparing or filing documents with the USPTO until reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement and notice obligations under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58
rubrics_metrics.description: As conditions for reinstatement, and to comply with § 11.58, Respondent must (for foreign-domiciled clients with immediate/prospective business before the Office) email the requisite § 11.58 notices and information (including a correctly translated Final Order) to clients in the client's native language and follow procedures to ensure delivery and attest to reasonable measures in affidavits/petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options for emailing: (1) email address listed in Applicant’s Information if belonging to client and directly accessible; (2) an email address belonging to client with direct access; or (3) to referring foreign third party only if reasonable measures ensure prompt forwarding to client, confirmation of receipt, and affidavit/petition details documenting measures. Additional reinstatement conditions include completing 4 hours CLE on legal ethics, reviewing TMEP signature provisions, and completing USPTO Trademark Basics Boot Camp modules, plus probation and reporting obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED publication and Official Gazette notice expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Orders resolving disciplinary matters will be published by the OED (e.g., FOIA reading room) and a notice materially consistent with the provided text will be published in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public dissemination is part of disciplinary process and warns other practitioners about expected standards (e.g., signature rules, sponsorship duties, supervision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney duty to cooperate with USPTO investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall cooperate fully with USPTO inquiries into improper filings by entities and persons with whom the respondent worked in connection with trademark documents submitted to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation examples include providing itemized lists of associated filings and participating in interviews; cooperation can be a mitigating consideration in discipline.
